title: Speed of Sound, Frequency, and Wavelength
lead: Sound travels at a definite speed, and its frequency and wavelength are tied to that speed as they are for every wave. This section names the perception of frequency pitch, relates the speed of sound to its frequency and wavelength, shows how the speed depends on the medium and on the temperature of the air, and explains why the speed of sound is nearly the same for every frequency.
objectives: Describe the relationship between the speed of sound, its frequency, and its wavelength.
Describe the effects on the speed of sound as it travels through various media.
Describe the effects of temperature on the speed of sound.
summary_html:
• The relationship of the speed of sound $\kvw$, its frequency $\kf$, and its wavelength $\klam$ is given by $\kvw = \kf\klam,$ which is the same relationship given for all waves.
  • In air, the speed of sound is related to air temperature $\kTemp$ by $\kvw = (331\ \text{m/s})\sqrt{\frac{\kTemp}{273\ \text{K}}}.$
  • $\kvw$ is the same for all frequencies and wavelengths.

figures.original_caption: A sound wave emanates from a source vibrating at a frequency f, propagates at v_w, and has a wavelength λ.
A bat uses sound echoes to find its way about and to catch prey. The time for the echo to return is directly proportional to the distance.

Because they travel at the same speed in a given medium, low-frequency sounds must have a greater wavelength than high-frequency sounds. Here, the lower-frequency sounds are emitted by the large speaker, called a woofer, while the higher-frequency sounds are emitted by the small speaker, called a tweeter.

exercises.prompt: Imagine you observe two fireworks explode. You hear the explosion of one as soon as you see it. However, you see the other firework for several milliseconds before you hear the explosion. Explain why this is so.

answer.solution: Sound and light both travel at definite speeds. The speed of sound is slower than the speed of light. The first firework is probably very close by, so the speed difference is not noticeable. The second firework is farther away, so the light arrives at your eyes noticeably sooner than the sound wave arrives at your ears.

exercises.prompt: You observe two musical instruments that you cannot identify. One plays high-pitch sounds and the other plays low-pitch sounds. How could you determine which is which without hearing either of them play?

answer.solution: Compare their sizes. High-pitch instruments are generally smaller than low-pitch instruments because they generate a smaller wavelength.

exercises.prompt:
A teacher wants to demonstrate that the speed of sound is not a constant value. Considering her regular classroom voice as the control, which of the following will increase the speed of sound leaving her mouth?
  1. Submerge her mouth underwater and speak at the same volume.
  2. Increase the temperature of the room and speak at the same volume.
  3. Increase the pitch of her voice and speak at the same volume.

answer.hint: The speed of sound is set by the medium and its temperature, not by the frequency of the source. Which of the three changes alters the medium or its temperature?

exercises.prompt:
All members of an orchestra begin tuning their instruments at the same time. While some woodwind instruments play high frequency notes, other stringed instruments play notes of lower frequency. Yet an audience member will hear all notes simultaneously, in apparent contrast to the equation.
Explain how a student could demonstrate the flaw in the above logic, using a slinky, stopwatch, and meter stick. Make sure to explain what relationship is truly demonstrated in the above equation, in addition to what would be necessary to get the speed of the slinky to actually change. You may include diagrams and equations as part of your explanation.

answer.solution: The flaw is in reading $\kvw = \kf\klam$ as if the speed depended on the frequency. In a given medium the speed of a wave is fixed by the medium, so the equation says that the frequency and the wavelength must adjust to each other: a higher frequency means a shorter wavelength, and their product is always the same speed. A student can show this with a slinky stretched to a fixed length along the floor. Shake one end slowly and then quickly, sending waves of two different frequencies down the same slinky, and time each with the stopwatch as it travels a distance measured with the meter stick. The speed comes out the same for both, while the meter stick shows that the fast shaking produces a shorter wavelength than the slow shaking. To make the speed of the wave change, the medium itself must change: stretch the slinky to a greater tension, or use a heavier or lighter slinky. Then the same shaking gives a different speed, and the wavelength changes with it, which is exactly why every instrument of the orchestra, high or low, is heard at once.

exercises.prompt: How do sound vibrations of atoms differ from thermal motion?

answer.solution: Thermal motion is random. Each atom or molecule moves in its own direction at its own speed, the average of those speeds is the rms speed $\kvrms = \sqrt{3k\kTemp/m}$, and because the directions are random there is no net motion of the gas. A sound vibration is an organized motion added on top of the thermal motion: the atoms of a region move together, back and forth along the direction the sound travels, so that compressions and rarefactions pass through the medium at the speed of sound with a definite frequency and wavelength. The two are connected, since the speed at which the disturbance can be passed from particle to particle depends on how fast the particles are already moving, which is why the speed of sound in a gas grows with the square root of the temperature, but the sound vibration is coherent and the thermal motion is not.

exercises.prompt: When sound passes from one medium to another where its propagation speed is different, does its frequency or wavelength change? Explain your answer briefly.

answer.solution: The wavelength changes and the frequency does not. The sound in the second medium is driven by the vibrations arriving from the first, like a driven oscillation, so it has the frequency of the original source. Because $\kvw = \kf\klam$ and the speed is different in the second medium while the frequency is the same, the wavelength must change in the same proportion as the speed: the higher the speed of sound in the new medium, the longer the wavelength there.

exercises.prompt: When poked by a spear, an operatic soprano lets out a 1200-Hz shriek. What is its wavelength if the speed of sound is 345 m/s?
Calculate the speed of sound on a day when a 1500 Hz frequency has a wavelength of 0.221 m.

answer.hint: The speed is the product of the frequency and the wavelength.

exercises.prompt: Show that the speed of sound in $20.0^\circ\text{C}$ air is 343 m/s, as claimed in the text.
Dolphins make sounds in air and water. What is the ratio of the wavelength of a sound in air to its wavelength in seawater? Assume air temperature is $20.0^\circ\text{C}$.

answer.hint: The frequency is the same in both media, so the ratio of the wavelengths is the ratio of the speeds. Take the speed in seawater from Table 17.1 and the speed in air from the temperature formula.

exercises.prompt:
(a) If a submarine’s sonar can measure echo times with a precision of 0.0100 s, what is the smallest difference in distances it can detect? (Assume that the submarine is in the ocean, not in fresh water.)
(b) Discuss the limits this time resolution imposes on the ability of the sonar system to detect the size and shape of the object creating the echo.

answer.hint: An echo travels out and back, so a difference in echo time corresponds to twice the difference in distance. Use the speed of sound in sea water from Table 17.1.
answer.solution:
(a) 7.70 m
(b) This means that sonar is good for spotting and locating large objects, but it isn’t able to resolve smaller objects, or detect the detailed shapes of objects. Objects like ships or large pieces of airplanes can be found by sonar, while smaller pieces must be found by other means.

exercises.prompt: Suppose a bat uses sound echoes to locate its insect prey, 3.00 m away. (See Figure 17.9.) (a) Calculate the echo times for temperatures of $5.00^\circ\text{C}$ and $35.0^\circ\text{C}$. (b) What percent uncertainty does this cause for the bat in locating the insect? (c) Discuss the significance of this uncertainty and whether it could cause difficulties for the bat. (In practice, the bat continues to use sound as it closes in, eliminating most of any difficulties imposed by this and other effects, such as motion of the prey.)

parts.hint: Find the speed of sound at 278 K, then the echo travels 6.00 m in all.
Find the speed of sound at 308 K, then the echo travels 6.00 m in all.
Compare the difference between the two times with the time itself.

answer.solution:
(a) 18.0 ms, 17.1 ms
(b) 5.00%
(c) This uncertainty could definitely cause difficulties for the bat, if it didn’t continue to use sound as it closed in on its prey. A 5% uncertainty could be the difference between catching the prey around the neck or around the chest, which means that it could miss grabbing its prey.
